claims.text: Waves erode the coast in three ways: hydraulic action forces water and trapped air into cracks in the rock until the pressure loosens and breaks it; abrasion is the waves throwing sand and pebbles against the cliff face; corrosion is sea water slowly dissolving rock it can chemically attack, such as limestone.

claims.text: The sea transports material along the coast: waves that approach the beach at an angle throw material up the shore with the swash and drag it back with the backwash, so sand and shingle move along the coast bit by bit - a process called longshore drift; as pebbes travel they grind against one another and wear smaller and rounder, a process called attrition.

claims.text: Deposition happens where the water loses energy: waves drop sand and shingle in sheltered bays to build beaches, and longshore drift builds long ridges called spits across bay mouths and river corners; dry sand blown inland from a wide beach at low tide piles into coastal sand dunes, so beaches are built by the sea and dunes are built by the wind.

claims.text: The three erosion processes are told apart by how the rock breaks: hydraulic action breaks rock by pressure, abrasion breaks it by impact, and corrosion breaks it by dissolving - so an answer that swaps the descriptions has swapped the mechanisms, not just the names.

claims.text: A cliff retreats because waves attack its base with hydraulic action and abrasion; the undercut rock above collapses, and the fallen material is broken up and carried away, leaving a flat rocky wave-cut platform at the foot of the cliff as the cliff line moves inland.

claims.text: On a headland the sequence is crack, cave, arch, stack, stump: waves widen a crack into a cave, the cave breaks through the headland to form an arch, the arch roof collapses to leave a stack standing in the sea, and the stack is later worn down to a stump.

claims.text: Where bands of hard and soft rock meet the coast, the soft rock is eroded faster, leaving a bay, while the hard rock stands out as a headland; wave energy is concentrated on the headlands, so they erode, while the sheltered bays fill with deposited sand and shingle beaches.

claims.text: A spit forms where longshore drift carries sand and shingle past a sharp change in the coastline, such as a river mouth or a bay: the drifting material is deposited into deeper, slower water and builds a long ridge joined to the land at one end, curving where the wind or the waves change direction.

claims.text: A coral reef is a ridge of limestone built in shallow tropical seas by the stony skeletons of coral polyps, which keep single-celled algae inside their bodies and so need sunlight: reefs therefore grow where the water is warm (roughly 20 degrees Celsius or warmer), clear, shallow and salty.

claims.text: A mangrove swamp is a belt of mangrove trees growing in the mud of sheltered tropical coasts that the tide floods daily; the trees stand on tangled aerial roots that hold the mud and tolerate the salt, so mangrove swamps develop where the coast is sheltered, the water is muddy and the tide rises high enough to flood the ground.

claims.text: Coasts offer people opportunities: flat, low land for building; harbours where sheltered deep water lets ships trade; fishing grounds that give food and jobs; and beaches and scenery that draw visitors, whose spending supports hotels, restaurants and tour operators.

claims.text: Coasts present hazards: storm winds and low pressure raise the sea into a storm surge that floods low-lying coastal land; waves erode cliffs and narrow beaches, undermining homes and roads; and tropical storms bring destructive winds and heavy rain as well as the surge.

claims.text: A tropical storm causes coastal flooding through a chain: its low pressure and strong onshore winds raise the sea into a storm surge, so the sea floods inland over low-lying ground, which means salt water and silt are left on farmland, so crops fail and the season's harvest is lost to the floodwater rather than the wind.

claims.text: Hard defences each work in their own way: a sea wall reflects wave energy back out to sea; rock armour at the cliff foot absorbs the energy of breaking waves in the gaps between its boulders; and groynes trap the sand that longshore drift moves along the beach, so the beach keeps its width and the wide beach itself takes the day-to-day wave energy.

claims.text: Soft management works with the sand rather than against the waves: beach nourishment adds sand trucked or pumped onto the shore, so the beach is widened, which has to be repeated because storms remove the sand again; managed retreat moves buildings and uses out of the zone the sea can reach, so the coast absorbs wave energy without the cost of defending every metre.
